title: Historic Preservation
summary: Indigenous historic preservation on Long Island protects burial places, cultural landscapes, community buildings, records, and other places whose meaning continues in Native communities. New York law now establishes procedures for discoveries of unmarked human remains and funerary objects outside regulated cemeteries.
content:
Preservation and Living Communities

Indigenous preservation begins with living communities. A cultural landscape may remain important even when its history is not visible in a standing building. Burial places, shorelines, meeting grounds, paths, churches, homes, language records, and places of work can all carry continuing relationships and responsibilities.

Native nations and culturally affiliated communities hold knowledge that is not contained in archaeological reports or property records. Their participation is essential when preservation decisions affect ancestors, funerary belongings, sacred places, or community history.

New York's Unmarked Burial Site Protection Law

New York's Unmarked Burial Site Protection Act took effect on June 28, 2023. It is now codified in Executive Law Section 171. The law establishes a process for reporting human remains or funerary objects found outside a regulated cemetery, stopping disturbance, notifying the appropriate authorities, consulting culturally affiliated groups, and determining respectful care and disposition.

The law also created a Native American Burial Site Review Committee and established civil and criminal penalties for prohibited disturbance, removal, concealment, or sale. It does not make every preservation conflict simple, but it provides protections that New York lacked for many years.

Preservation on Long Island

Long Island preservation work includes Native-led land defense, burial protection, restoration of community buildings, legal advocacy, archival research, and efforts to keep culturally important landscapes from being destroyed or misrepresented. The histories connected with Parrish Pond, Canoe Place Chapel, the Jamesport burial agreement, Shinnecock Hills, and other places show that preservation can involve direct action as well as legislation.

Some locations remain broad or undisclosed because public directions could place ancestors, ceremonies, archaeological deposits, or private land at risk. Protecting a place can also mean respecting a community's decision not to publish every detail.

Sources

  • New York Executive Law Section 171, Protection of Unmarked Burial Sites.
  • New York State Assembly, New Laws Taking Effect in 2023, pp. 4-5.
  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here! The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today, 2nd ed. (1998).

Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

What can archaeology contribute to Indigenous Long Island history, and what are its limits?

Archaeology provides physical evidence of Indigenous daily life, trade, and continuous land use, disrupting colonial narratives of early Native disappearance. However, its limits include site destruction from urban development and the inability of physical objects to replace living oral traditions.

Archaeological research on Long Island offers invaluable material evidence of pre-contact and historic Indigenous life, directly filling the gaps left by silent or biased colonial records. As discussed in Ralph Solecki's 'Archaeological Position of Fort Corchaug' (1950) and Allison Manfra McGovern's 'Disrupting the Narrative' (2015), physical excavations of sites like Fort Corchaug and historic homesteads recover tools, shells, animal bones, and pottery that reconstruct daily domestic labor, trade networks, and adaptive economic survivance. Despite these contributions, archaeology has major limitations. Extensive agricultural plowing, shoreline erosion, and rapid suburban development have destroyed or fragmented many crucial sites. Furthermore, a long history of unregulated looting and unscientific hobbyist digging has stripped away context and commodified cultural materials. Most importantly, physical artifacts alone cannot convey the spiritual, linguistic, and cultural meanings of the landscape. Modern public history rejects the dated practice of treating archaeological materials as isolated collectibles or letting scientific classifications override living community knowledge. Truly ethical archaeology must be conducted in close partnership with sovereign tribal nations, prioritizing community-led research protocols and protecting sensitive ancestral spaces.

Sources

  • Ralph S. Solecki and Lorraine E. Williams, Fort Corchaug Archaeological Site National Historic Landmark (1998), pp. 24-27.
  • Allison Manfra McGovern, Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montaukett (2015), pp. 10, 43-44.
  • Gaynell Stone, The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), pp. 11-12.
What can preservation laws and public agencies do, and where do they fall short?

Preservation laws and agencies can review projects, protect some public sites, document discoveries, and support repatriation, but coverage varies by land ownership, jurisdiction, and the type of resource. Legal compliance is a minimum; early consultation and Native-led decision-making provide stronger protection.

Federal, state, tribal, and local preservation systems do not all cover the same land or activity. Environmental review, local landmark rules, archaeological conditions, cemetery law, and repatriation requirements can each help in particular circumstances, yet gaps remain—especially when a place is unmarked, privately owned, poorly documented, or discovered after work begins. Agencies can improve outcomes by consulting Native Nations early, protecting confidential location data, requiring qualified investigation, and treating avoidance and preservation as priorities rather than waiting for emergency discovery.

Sources

  • Suffolk County Archaeological Association Newsletter, Vol. 46 No. 3 (2020).
  • Suffolk County Archaeological Association Vol. 49, No. 1 (2023).
  • Gaynell Stone, The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), p. 11.
  • Margo Thunderbird, Aftermath: Shinnecocks Propose New Laws For Native American Burial Sites (2004).
why_this_matters: Preservation is not only about old buildings or objects. Native communities protect ancestors, homelands, gathering places, language, memory, and the right to decide how culturally important places are understood and cared for.
